Field surveys of Boarfish (Capros aper) in the northeastern Atlantic have provided key demographic data for this small-bodied zeiform species. Studies on female specimens indicate that sexual maturation begins when individuals reach a total length of 9.7 cm [Lp = 9.7 cm]. The mass of females at this pubertal transition has been estimated at 15.2 grams [Wwp = 15.2 grams], a value derived from length–weight relationships established for the species. At the other end of the size spectrum, the ultimate total length achieved by females reaches 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], which corresponds to an asymptotic wet body mass of 420 grams [Wwi = 420 grams]. These upper bounds were recorded from long-term trawl surveys and are thought to represent the maximum attainable size under natural conditions in the region. The growth trajectory from puberty to the asymptotic size appears to be gradual, consistent with the life history of a relatively slow-growing benthic fish.

Reproductive output in Boarfish has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. At this thermal regime, females produce approximately 63 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 63 eggs per spawning event], and these spawning events occur around once per day [F_R_i = events occur around once per day], reflecting a reproductive strategy that balances moderate batch fecundity with sustained spawning effort over time. The maximum daily reproductive rate, therefore, integrates a small clutch size with a daily spawning pattern, a strategy unusual among temperate marine teleosts. This intense reproductive schedule is thought to compensate for high rates of egg and larval mortality in the planktonic environment. The microscopic eggs, which are pelagic and transparent, have a diameter of roughly 1 mm, leading to an estimated wet weight at birth for the newly hatched yolk-sac larva of just 0.00078 grams [Wwb = 0.00078 grams].

Lifespan estimates for Capros aper have been derived from otolith-based age readings of wild-caught individuals. Under the ambient thermal conditions of their natural habitat, which average approximately 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the oldest documented individuals reach a maximum lifespan of 30 years [am = 30 years]. This impressive longevity, exceeding three decades, is notable for a fish that attains a maximum body mass of less than half a kilogram and suggests a very slow rate of physiological aging. The extended lifespan is likely linked to the species' low metabolic demands and its occupation of relatively stable, cool, deep-water environments on the continental slope. Such a long reproductive window, spanning many years, allows for repeated spawning events across the adult life of each individual, contributing to overall population persistence despite potentially low juvenile survival rates.

The timing of first reproduction in Boarfish has been documented in relation to age and body size under the species' typical thermal regime of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. The age at first successful spawning event is approximately 3.4 years after hatching [tR = approximately 3.4 years after hatching], a protracted juvenile period that corresponds with the attainment of the pubertal length of 9.7 cm at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This delay between hatching and first reproduction reflects the substantial time required for the larvae to progress through the planktonic phase, undergo metamorphosis, and then grow as benthic juveniles to the reproductive size threshold. The transition from an endotrophic yolk-sac larva to an exogenously feeding pelagic larva is a critical period, and the relatively late age at first spawning implies a conservative life history strategy typical of long-lived marine fishes with low natural adult mortality.

The larval-juvenile transition in Capros aper involves a pronounced allometric shift in body shape and fin ray ossification. Newly hatched prolarvae, weighing only 0.00078 grams [Wwb = 0.00078 grams], are lecithotrophic and rely entirely on yolk reserves until mouth opening and first prey capture.
